sections.body_en:
When Israel left Egypt, many converts joined them, as it is stated (Shemot 12:37-38): "The children of Israel journeyed from Ramses to Sukkot, about six hundred thousand men on foot, besides children. And a mixed multitude (erev rav) also went up with them." These converts sought to convert after they saw the great power of God, who sent Moshe to take His people Israel out of Egypt. And God Himself also guided Moshe our teacher to accept them. "God said: Whoever loves My children, let him come and rejoice with My children. The worthy ones in Egypt came and performed the Pesaḥ with Israel and went up with them, as it is stated: 'And a mixed multitude also went up with them'" (Shemot Rabba 18:10). This is what was said to Israel in Egypt (Shemot 12:48-49): "When a stranger (ger) shall dwell with you and would perform the Pesaḥ to the Lord, let all his males be circumcised, and then he may draw near to perform it, and he shall be as a native of the land; but no uncircumcised person shall eat of it. There shall be one law for the native and for the stranger who dwells among you" (Ramban, Bamidbar 9:14). With the joining of the converts in Egypt, one of the purposes of the Egyptian exile was realised, and the promise that God made to Avraham our father was fulfilled: "And afterward they shall go out with great wealth"; the great wealth included the converts as well (Bereshit 15:14; Panim Yafot there 15:13; Sefat Emet, Bo 5643).

Apparently, there were Egyptians who already from the time Moshe began his mission sought to join Israel, and it was clear that they were righteous and fit to be converted. As the plagues intensified, the stature of Moshe, the messenger of God, grew greater and greater in the eyes of the Egyptians, as it is stated (Shemot 11:3): "Moreover, the man Moshe was very great in the land of Egypt, in the eyes of Pharaoh's servants and in the eyes of the people," and as a result those seeking to convert multiplied greatly. And God said to Moshe (Shemot 7:4): "And I will bring out My hosts, My people the children of Israel," implying without many converts, but Moshe our teacher said: "It is good that converts cleave to the Shekhina," and accepted them (Rashi, Shemot 32:7). And they were the ones who caused Israel to sin with the sin of the Golden Calf, near Mount Sinai. Then God said to Moshe (Shemot 32:7): "Go, get down, for your people, whom you brought up out of the land of Egypt, have acted corruptly." The Sages said (Shemot Rabba 42:6): "Moshe said: Master of the universe, how are they my people?! The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: They are your people, for while they were still in Egypt I told you not to mix a mixed multitude among them; you, who were humble and upright, said to Me: Those who return are always accepted. And I knew what they would do in the future; I said to you: No, and I did your will. And they are the ones who made the Calf, for they were idol worshippers, and they made it and caused My people to sin."

The Zohar explains (2:191a) that among the erev rav there were also Egyptian sorcerers and magicians, who, after they saw that God's might was above all their sorcery, submitted to God and sought to join Israel. And God warned Moshe not to accept them. Moshe said to God: "Master of the worlds, since they have seen Your mighty deeds they wish to convert; let them see Your mighty deeds every day and know that there is no God besides You." Since after Moshe's response God did not instruct Moshe not to accept them, Moshe our teacher, the servant of God, trusted in all His house, accepted them. And when Moshe delayed in coming down from the mountain after the giving of the Torah, these converts of the erev rav lost faith that he would return, and they were the ones who sought to make a statue through which they could connect to God and to the legacy of Moshe, and they were the ones who, by their sorcery, caused the gold that Aharon melted down to become a calf, and they were the ones who said to Israel: "These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt" (Shemot 32:4 and Rashi; Vayikra Rabba 27:8). Afterward, too, the erev rav continued to cause Israel to sin, as it is stated (Bamidbar 11:4): "And the riffraff (asafsuf) that was among them fell to lusting, and the children of Israel also wept again and said: Who will give us meat to eat?" The riffraff are people of the erev rav (Bamidbar Rabba 15:24; Rashi; Rambam, Hilkhot Issurei Bi'ah 13:18).1

notes_en.en:
Most of the erev rav were Egyptians; however, since Egypt was an empire, there were members of other nations in it, and some of them also converted, and therefore all the converts were called erev rav – a mixture of many nations (see Zohar 2:191a, and Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Ha-ketav Ve-ha-kabbala on Shemot 12:38).
In the Mekhilta de-Rabbi Yishmael and the Mekhilta de-Rabbi Shimon bar Yoḥai, opinions are cited regarding the number of the erev rav, from 120 ten-thousands (1,200,000) up to 360 ten-thousands (3,600,000), and in the Tanḥuma (Ki Tisa 19) they said that there were forty thousand. The Maharal explained that numbers in the words of Ḥazal are often meant to express an idea and not as historical documentation (see Gevurot Hashem 12). In any case, we have learned that the erev rav were many. At the same time, the Sages said (Mekhilta de-Rabbi Yishmael, Shemot 13:18) that only a fifth of the people left Egypt and all the rest died, as it is stated (Shemot 13:18): "And the children of Israel went up armed (ḥamushim) out of the land of Egypt," because many of Israel were wicked and did not want to leave Egypt, and God put them to death during the three days of gloom of the plague of darkness, so that the Egyptians would not see their downfall and the name of Heaven would not be desecrated.
In the Mekhilta (Parashat Ha-shira 1) it is explained that "your people have acted corruptly" refers to Israel, and they were called Moshe's "people" "because he gave his life for them." Whereas in Shemot Rabba 42:6 and in Rashi, Shemot 32:7, it is explained that it was the erev rav who were called Moshe's "people," because Moshe accepted them without God's recommendation. One can explain that "your people" includes all of Israel, for whom Moshe gave his life, and in a special way the erev rav whom he converted.
Some say that Israel and the erev rav stood together at the assembly at Mount Sinai, for God cherished the members of the nations as well at Sinai, as it is stated (Devarim 33:3-4): "Indeed, He loves the peoples; all His holy ones are in Your hand, and they sat down at Your feet, receiving of Your words. Moshe commanded us a Torah, an inheritance of the congregation of Yaakov" (Rashbam there). And some say that it is possible that Israel stood in front of the erev rav, for the Torah was given to Israel (Ramban, Shemot 19:1-2). Similarly, some say that the place of the erev rav in the wilderness was outside the camp of Israel, and the Clouds of Glory did not rest upon them, and the manna did not fall for them, and nevertheless they ate manna from what was left over (Zohar 2:191b), and the meaning is that the level of their eating was lower. However, even according to the Zohar (3:237a), part of the erev rav truly attached itself to Israel, to the point that many members of the tribe of Shimon married them, and many of them were killed at Shittim, and it became clear that they were not fit to be Israelites. It was further explained that there was a dispute between Israel and the erev rav over their share in the spoils of Egypt (Lekaḥ Tov, Shemot 18:13). The Zohar further says (2:195a; Ra'aya Mehemna 3:237b) that at first all of Israel and the erev rav were called upon to contribute to the Mishkan, as it is stated (Shemot 25:2): "from every man whose heart makes him willing," and after the sin of the Calf the call was: "Take from among you… the congregation of the children of Israel" alone (ibid. 35:4-5). For only after they separated from the erev rav could they lift up their heads and contribute to the Mishkan (Zohar 3:237b).

sections.title_en: The Good and the Complications in the Erev Rav
sections.body_en:
The aim of the Exodus from Egypt was to bring out to freedom Israel and all the converts joining them, and thereby to redeem all the holy sparks that were imprisoned in the prison of materialism and enslaved to wickedness. For every additional spark that went out with them to freedom added great light, whereas, had it remained imprisoned in Egypt, it would have continued to give its strength to the kingdom of wickedness.

The Arizal explained that the root of the souls of the erev rav is in Israel, but at the time of the Exodus from Egypt many of them had not yet reached the stage appropriate, ideally (le-khatḥila), for their conversion and rectification. Therefore at first God did not want Moshe to convert them (Sha'ar Ha-pesukim, p. 107). However, when Moshe our teacher sought to convert them, God did not object, for although the matter involves complications and suffering, the rectification that would grow out of it is great, for through it these holy sparks would not be lost from Israel, and the name of God would be magnified and sanctified and blessing would increase in the world.

In order to understand the complications that intensified in the wake of accepting the erev rav, one must explain that the process of the rectification of the world (tikkun olam) involves many clarifications that take place in stages. At every stage new trials arise, and from the depths of the soul and its abysses there rise good desires and ideas together with evil dross, and the more Israel cleave to the Torah, the more they merit to deepen the revelation of the good and to overcome the trials, and the evil dross separates from them, and they merit to be purified and elevated. And when they do not merit, the evil dross prevails, and according to the measure of its prevailing – many of Israel are enticed, sin and fall. And out of the troubles and suffering caused by this, the good is revealed and the evil dross separates, and Israel continue to grow to the next stage. Through the joining of the erev rav, Israel merited to elevate further great sparks, but for this they had to contend with harsher dross. So it was at the giving of the Torah: on the one hand, thanks to the erev rav the Torah was revealed on a higher level, and Yitro, the greatest of the erev rav, even added a passage to the Torah. On the other hand, under the influence of the erev rav they also sinned and underwent greater crises.2

notes_en.en:
The exile in Egypt was meant to elevate converts, both in that all of Israel who went up from Egypt are called "converts," and through the addition of the erev rav. The Arizal explained in Sha'ar Ha-pesukim, p. 103, that Israel in Egypt were a reincarnation of the generation of the Flood, who sinned by wasting seed, and of the generation of the Dispersion, who made bricks to build a tower, and they were rectified in Egypt through the drowning of the children in water and through the hard labour with bricks. And there, p. 107, it is explained that the enslavement in Egypt was meant for the rectification of Israel, and Israel were more refined and the erev rav less so, and because of Moshe's exalted stature he wished to bring the erev rav close as well, for they are sparks of the aspect of "Da'at" (knowledge), the level of Moshe, but he was punished on their account "because the time of their rectification had not yet come, and he wished to rectify them before their time."
Rav Pinḥas Halevi, author of the Hafla'a, wrote in Panim Yafot (Bereshit 15:13): "The essence of the Egyptian exile was to clarify the holy sparks that fell through the sin of the Tree of Knowledge, as Ḥazal said (Pesaḥim 87b): Israel was exiled only so that converts would be added to them, that is, holy sparks that are gathered one by one over the course of the exile." And thereby they rectified the sparks of Da'at that had been scattered; and had they merited to reveal Da'at, the converts would have come of their own accord, but when they did not merit, and Avraham said "How shall I know?" (ba-meh eda), and continued the sin of the Tree of Knowledge – they had to go down into exile in order to rectify Da'at, as it is stated (Bereshit 15:13): "Know for certain that your offspring shall be strangers (ger)"; and so he wrote there, Shemot 11:2. And so he wrote in the Hafla'a commentary on the Pesaḥ Haggada ("Ve-Lavan bikesh"), that the converts are the inner essence of the great wealth with which Israel left Egypt, and therefore we must give thanks for the exiles as for the redemptions, for through the exiles converts join. And in his book Ha-mikneh (Kiddushin 70b) he wrote that although the converts come by virtue of the holy spark, it is impossible that a little refuse should not cling to them, and one must take care that they do not have a bad influence on Israel, as happened with the erev rav. And so he wrote in Panim Yafot (Devarim 7:1; 17) that the greater Israel are, the more they are able to absorb holy sparks without being drawn after the refuse clinging to them. And so wrote Rabbi Tzadok in Dover Tzedek, p. 111. And there, p. 200, he wrote: "And in all of Israel's good gifts there were also converts; at the time of the giving of the Torah there was the erev rav, and their root was Yitro, whose name is mentioned in the Torah; and likewise at the gift of the land there were many, and their root was Raḥav" (see Shir Ha-shirim Rabba 1:3:3). And so in Sefat Emet, Yitro 5652, and in Parashat Bo 5643: "For it is known that the children of Israel elevated from Egypt holy sparks that were found there, as it is written: like the garden of the Lord, like the land of Egypt." And he explains that the great wealth caused the sin of the Calf, both the gold and silver and the erev rav. For "great labour was needed to rectify them and to refine them refinement after refinement. Indeed, certainly everything will be rectified… until the future redemption, and this is the praise, that they did according to the word of Moshe."

sections.title_en: The Dross of the Erev Rav in Jewish History
sections.body_en:
Throughout the generations, when the Sages saw Jews who behaved with cruelty and wickedness and did not have compassion for others, they concluded that apparently the evil side of the erev rav that had not yet been rectified had prevailed in them. As is told of Shabtai bar Marinus, who came to a Jewish community in Babylonia, and the local people did not agree to include him in their business and their work, and also did not agree to give him food to eat. He said: "These are descended from the erev rav." For the rule is: "Whoever has compassion for people – it is known that he is of the seed of Avraham our father, and whoever does not have compassion for people – it is known that he is not of the seed of Avraham our father" (Beitza 32b).

Although according to halakha anyone whose mother is Jewish is Jewish, the Sages recommended not to marry someone who lacks the three traits characteristic of Israel: 1) compassionate, 2) bashful, that is, God-fearing people who are not brazen, 3) performers of kindness (Yevamot 79a; SA EH 2:2). That is to say, today the erev rav are not particular people, but rather bad traits and dross mixed into the souls of Israel. For since many generations have already passed since the erev rav converted and intermingled with Israel, it is reasonable that every Jew is also among the descendants of the erev rav. And when one sees Jews in whom the bad sides prevail, one should assume that the evil side of the erev rav, which has not yet been rectified or separated from Israel, has prevailed in them.

The kabbalists dealt at length with the subject of the erev rav, and explained that the main wickedness of the dross of the erev rav is expressed in Jews who hate their people, deny the special quality (segula) of Israel and join the enemies of Israel (Ma'amarei Ha-Re'iya, p. 60). And if they do not awaken to repent, they will separate from the nation and be erased from Israel through death or assimilation. And when all the holy sparks in the erev rav are rectified and reveal in Israel the good in them, and all the souls of Israel scattered among the nations convert and return to the rock from which they were hewn, and, on the other hand, the dross of the erev rav is lost or separates from Israel, Israel will be able to reveal the full light of their Torah and to bring blessing to all the nations of the world.3

notes_en.en:
The Zohar says (1:25a-b) that there are five kinds of erev rav mixed among Israel, and because of them the Shekhina is in exile. 1) "Amalekites," and they are the harshest and most evil of the erev rav, and from them arise leaders who rule over Israel with cruelty, with instruments of violence in their hands. 2) "Nefilim," who sin with sexual immorality. 3) "Gibborim" (mighty men), who sin with arrogance, and build synagogues and study halls not for the sake of Heaven but in order to take pride, and rule over Israel, and especially rule over and rob the poor of Israel. 4) "Refa'im," who are slack (mitrapim) in helping Israel, and their main desire is to benefit the nations of the world. And even when Israel are in distress and they are able to help them, they do not share in their suffering and do not save them. And even when they are able to support those who study Torah, they are slack and do not support them. 5) "Anakim" (giants), who disparage Torah scholars and humiliate them. The Gra summarised five kinds of erev rav briefly: 1) people of strife and lashon ha-ra (evil speech), 2) people of lust, 3) hypocrites, 4) pursuers of honour, 5) pursuers of money. And he wrote that the worst of them, who are called "Amalekites," are the people of strife, "and the son of David will not come until they are erased from the world" (Even Shelema 11:8).
The kabbalists explained that all the sins in Israel stem from the erev rav, for the soul of Israel is holy and bound to God with an absolute and eternal bond, and only because of foreign influences are there Jews who act wickedly. And after all the dross of the erev rav separates from Israel and is lost, the people of Israel will be able to reveal the unity of God in the world, and the divine abundance will flow to the world and the redemption will come. However, as stated, without the conversion of all the converts, including the erev rav, all the holy sparks will not be elevated and the redemption will not come.

sections.title_en: Moshe Our Teacher and the Level of the Great Tzaddikim
sections.body_en:
As we have learned, although at first God warned Moshe our teacher not to convert all of the erev rav, Moshe our teacher, the faithful servant of God, decided to convert them. For he held that one should not reject someone who wishes to convert, and if they were put off until the time when they would be fit to convert in the ideal manner, there was reason to fear that the opportunity would be lost, and when the time of their rectification arrived there would be no opportunity to convert them, and Israel would have to undergo many exiles and sufferings in order to bring them back. And God did not object, for in truth this was God's will, that Moshe our teacher should volunteer of his own accord to convert them, and devote himself wholeheartedly to them in order to reveal the good hidden within them.

Through the self-sacrifice of Moshe our teacher for the community of Israel, and for those connected to Israel, including the erev rav, Moshe our teacher revealed God's will that no good life-force should be lost. And despite all the suffering and complications that would be caused by this, thanks to their joining the community of Israel, the word of God and His blessing would be revealed on a higher level. And likewise in all the generations, the great Torah scholars, who continue the path of Moshe our teacher, the faithful shepherds, lovers of Israel, who desire the complete revelation of the Torah and the sanctification of God's name in the world – devote themselves wholeheartedly to gathering all the holy sparks, and bring close both those who are distant and converts. Admittedly, the process is complicated, but precisely through it the words of the Torah are revealed in the deepest and most clarified manner.

The Arizal further said that at the end of the generations, in the "footsteps of the Messiah" (ikveta di-meshiḥa), the redemption depends on the rectification of all the souls of converts who are on the level of erev rav, which on the one hand are in practice on a low level, and on the other hand their root is very high, on the level of the depth of the supernal knowledge (da'at) of Moshe our teacher. And since they are connected to the root of the soul of Moshe our teacher, Moshe our teacher did not enter the Land, but remained outside the Land, until they all return to join Israel.4

notes_en.en:
Moshe our teacher was "generous of eye," for the Sages said (Nedarim 38a): "The Torah was given only to Moshe and his descendants… Moshe acted generously with it and gave it to Israel, and of him the verse says (Mishlei 22:9): He who has a generous eye shall be blessed, for he gives of his bread to the poor." Therefore he also brought the erev rav close (see note 2). However, the sins of the erev rav were also found in Israel, and therefore they all died in the wilderness, and Moshe our teacher gave his life for all of them, and was buried with them outside the Land in order to bring them with him at the completion of the rectification (see Devarim Rabba 2:9; Zohar 2:157a; the Arizal, Sha'ar Ha-pesukim, p. 107). It further emerges from the Arizal in Likkutei Torah, Va-etḥanan, "Va-yit'aber Hashem bi," that toward the end of the generations, the rectification descends to the level of the heel, and then most souls are of the aspect of erev rav. And it seems that since their root is in the aspect of Moshe's "Da'at," when they are rectified their stature will be extremely high. And Moshe remained outside the Land, in the aspect of the supernal Land of Israel whose influence is upon the whole world, and thereby he arouses in distant souls a longing for repentance toward the revelation of the Shekhina in the Land (see Shemona Kevatzim 7:14). And so wrote our master Rav Kook in Letter 555, that the great ones of the generations who walk in the path of Moshe our teacher bring the distant close and devote themselves to them, just as he devoted himself to the erev rav. And in Shemona Kevatzim 2:115, that the messianic aspect of Moshe our teacher is to bring close even those of lesser worth and the erev rav. And so he wrote there, 7:137-138, that this is how the disciples of Moshe our teacher act in all generations. And there, 1:326: "Every great soul is involved with all the branches that branch out from its roots, and it must rectify their defects, and it has the right to bring close the distant even more than is strictly proper, when it recognises that they belong to it." And the greater a person is, the more his branches extend to distant places and are all-inclusive, like Moshe our teacher and the great ones of the generations. And there, 2:35, that from the children of the brazen ones who break through boundaries great prophets will arise from the supernal level of Moshe our teacher, and the depth of the good will be revealed through them. And see Ein Aya, Shabbat, chapter 2, 79-80.
And so we learned in the Zohar (2:45b; see also 2:191a) that God took the erev rav into account, and therefore, although at first the plan was that Israel would enter the Land by the short route, by way of the land of the Philistines, since the erev rav had joined them, and there was a concern that out of fear of war with the Philistines and the Canaanites they would return to Egypt, God instructed all of Israel to go around and lengthen their journey by way of the wilderness and the Sea of Reeds, so that in the meantime the erev rav would be strengthened in their faith together with Israel. It further appears from the Zohar that Moshe our teacher gave his life mainly for the erev rav, for since the Zohar explained that they were the ones who sinned with the sin of the Calf, the decree of annihilation was mainly against them and against those of Israel who were drawn after them. Thus it was about the erev rav that God said to Moshe our teacher (Shemot 32:10): "Now therefore let Me alone, that My anger may burn against them and that I may consume them; and I will make of you a great nation." And by this He hinted to Moshe that the matter depended on him: if he did not exert himself to save them – the attribute of judgement would prevail, and God would have to annihilate them. Moshe understood that it was in his power to save them, and he gave his life for them, and after he punished all the sinners and eradicated the idolatry, he said to God (ibid. 32:32): "And now, if You will forgive their sin – and if not, blot me, I pray, out of Your book which You have written." Thereby Moshe agreed to give his life for them in this world and in the World to Come, for whoever is blotted out of God's book is blotted out forever from all the worlds.

sections.body_en:
The Sages said (Yerushalmi Shevi'it 6:1) that as Israel was about to enter the Land, Yehoshua bin Nun sent a notice to the Canaanites that, by the command of God, Israel was about to inherit the Land, and that three options stood before them:
1) Those who wish to move to another land – let them move. 2) Those who wish to remain in peace may remain with the status of ger toshav (resident alien), that is, they must undertake to observe the seven Noahide commandments, and undertake to be subject to the kingdom of Israel and to bear the public labours. And if they wish, they may even convert. 3) Those who wish to fight against Israel – let them fight, but let them know that Israel will fight them until their utter destruction. The Girgashites believed God and went to Africa and received a good land, while the rest of the Canaanites remained in their place and intended to fight against Israel.

After Israel began to conquer the Land, people came to them who claimed that they had come from a distant land because they had heard of the great miracles that God had performed for Israel, and they asked, in the name of their people, to make a covenant with Israel. In order that Israel would believe that they had come from a distant land, they wore worn-out clothes and provisioned themselves with old food. Without inquiring of God through the Urim and Tumim, the princes of Israel accepted their words and ate of their bread. "And Yehoshua made peace with them, and made a covenant with them to let them live, and the princes of the congregation swore to them" (Yehoshua 9:15). After three days it became clear that they were Canaanites of the Ḥivites, and that their cities, the most important of which was Givon, were within the territory of the inheritance of Binyamin.

Great resentment arose among Israel against the Givonim who had deceived them, and against the princes who had been enticed into making a covenant with them. However, the princes said to Israel: since we have sworn to them by God, we cannot touch them, but we can subjugate them. "And Yehoshua called them and spoke to them, saying: Why did you deceive us, saying, We are very far from you, when you dwell among us? Now therefore you are cursed, and there shall never cease to be of you bondmen, both hewers of wood and drawers of water for the house of my God. And they answered Yehoshua and said: Because it was certainly told your servants that the Lord your God commanded His servant Moshe to give you all the land and to destroy all the inhabitants of the land from before you; therefore we were greatly afraid for our lives because of you, and have done this thing. And now, behold, we are in your hand; as it seems good and right in your eyes to do to us, do. And so he did to them, and delivered them out of the hand of the children of Israel, and they did not kill them. And Yehoshua made them that day hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and for the altar of the Lord, to this day, in the place which He would choose" (ibid. 22-27). From then on, wherever the Mishkan was, the Givonim would supply the Mishkan with its needs: in Gilgal, in Shilo, in Nov, in Givon and in Jerusalem.

A short time later, the covenant that Israel made with the Givonim was put to the test. The Amorite Canaanite kings, who were angry at the Givonim for having betrayed them, went up against them to strike them. "And the men of Givon sent to Yehoshua, to the camp at Gilgal, saying: Do not slacken your hand from your servants; come up to us quickly, and save us, and help us, for all the kings of the Amorites who dwell in the hill country have gathered together against us" (Yehoshua 10:6). "At that moment Yehoshua said: Shall we trouble the public for the sake of these converts? The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: Yehoshua, if you distance those who are distant – you will end up distancing those who are near" (Bamidbar Rabba 8:4). And Israel went out to defend their allies the Givonim, and God helped them to defeat their enemies and to overwhelm them in a miraculous manner the like of which had never been. As it is stated (Yehoshua 10:10-14): "And the Lord threw them into confusion before Israel, and slew them with a great slaughter at Givon, and pursued them along the way of the ascent of Beit Ḥoron… And it came to pass, as they fled from before Israel, while they were in the descent of Beit Ḥoron, that the Lord cast down great stones from heaven upon them as far as Azeka, and they died; more died from the hailstones than those whom the children of Israel slew with the sword." Out of that tremendous elevation in the storm of battle, Yehoshua turned in prayer to God, asking Him to delay the setting of the sun, so that Israel could complete their victory: "Then Yehoshua spoke to the Lord on the day when the Lord delivered up the Amorites before the children of Israel, and he said in the sight of Israel: Sun, stand still upon Givon, and you, moon, in the valley of Ayalon. And the sun stood still, and the moon stayed, until the nation had avenged itself upon its enemies. Is it not written in the Book of Yashar? So the sun stood still in the midst of heaven, and did not hasten to go down for about a whole day. And there was no day like that before it or after it, that the Lord hearkened to the voice of a man, for the Lord fought for Israel."

In the opinion of many, the Givonim could have attained the status of ger toshav without deceiving. For as long as the war against them had not begun, they could have sued for peace and lived among Israel with the status of ger toshav, undertaking to meet two conditions: 1) to observe the seven Noahide commandments; 2) to accept the yoke of the kingdom of Israel by paying taxes and bearing the burden of public labours. But they thought that Israel would not accept them, and therefore they deceived Israel into thinking that they had come from a distant land, and they made a covenant with Israel as between two equal nations, and not as tribes subject to the rule of Israel. Israel resented their deceit, to the point that they sought to kill them like the rest of the Canaanites, the enemies of Israel. However, since they had made a covenant with them under oath, even though it was founded on deception, they did not want to desecrate the name of Heaven by breaking their oath, and they made peace with them as they would have done had they come honestly.

The Sages said that subsequently the Givonim were not content with the status of ger toshav, but converted and took upon themselves all the mitzvot like Israel. But since they had deceived, Yehoshua decreed that their law would be like that of slaves subjugated to the congregation and the altar, and they were called "Netinim," for they are given over (netunim) and subjugated to the service of the congregation and the altar, and Israel is forbidden to marry them. That is to say, although according to halakha they were not slaves, but rather had the status of converts who conduct their lives independently in their own cities, and accordingly they would be permitted to marry Israelites, Yehoshua decreed that they be considered as slaves, and just as an Israelite is forbidden to marry a male or female slave, so too it is forbidden to marry Givonim. However, since this prohibition stems from Yehoshua's decree, its level of severity is that of a rabbinic prohibition. In addition, Yehoshua did not issue his decree for all time, but left it pending. He said: "I neither distance them nor bring them close; rather, whoever will in the future build the Chosen House – whomever he decides to bring close, he will bring close, and whomever he decides to distance, he will distance. And David came and distanced them" (Yerushalmi Sanhedrin 6:7).[5]

notes_en.en:
Many hold that the Givonim could have sued for peace without deceiving, and they erred in this and therefore deceived (Rambam, Hilkhot Melakhim 6:5; Radak, Yehoshua 9:7; Malbim there 9:3). And some say that they wanted peace between equals, and therefore they deceived (Abarbanel, Yehoshua 9:15; see Ramban, Devarim 20:11). And some say that only before Israel crossed the Jordan could they have sued for peace, and since they were moved to sue for peace after Israel had crossed the Jordan, they were saved only through deceit (Ra'avad on the Rambam there, and Tosafot Gittin 46a, s.v. "kevan"). And according to the Yerushalmi (Kiddushin 4:1), the Givonim sought to make Israel stumble, and this is what they said: "We will go and deceive them, and they will make a covenant with us. Either way: if they kill us – they will have transgressed the oath; if they let us live – they will have transgressed the decree. Either way they will be punished and we will inherit the land."
According to the Rambam, in addition to the fact that the Canaanites could make peace under the conditions explained, they could also convert and marry Israelites (Hilkhot Issurei Bi'ah 12:22), and this is also the opinion of Rashi and the Ma'or. And according to the Ramban and Rashba, only the children of the converts were permitted to marry Israelites. However, since the Givonim deceived, Yehoshua decreed that they not marry even with their children, and the nature of the prohibition is rabbinic, and he based this on his ruling that they be considered slaves of the Mishkan, and since an Israelite is forbidden to marry slaves, it is forbidden to marry them (second explanation in Tosafot Yevamot 79a, s.v. "u-Netinim"). And according to Rabbeinu Tam, by Torah law it is forbidden to marry the descendants of Canaanite converts forever, and the decree of Yehoshua and David regarding the Givonim was that they be subjugated to Israel and to the labours of the Temple (based on the Rishonim on Yevamot 78b–79a, Ketubot 29a; Beit Shmuel 4:1. See below, note 20).
In Yevamot 79a it is explained that already Moshe our teacher accepted people like the Givonim to be hewers of wood and drawers of water, as it is stated (Devarim 29:9-10): "You are standing this day, all of you, before the Lord your God… and your stranger that is in the midst of your camp, from the hewer of your wood to the drawer of your water." And he accepted them for this because he saw that they were not suited to be full converts (Ramban there). Yehoshua acted toward the Givonim in accordance with this precedent.

sections.title_en: The Givonim in the Days of Shaul and David
sections.body_en:
About four hundred years passed, and David was already reigning over Israel. Toward the end of his reign, "there was a famine in the days of David for three years, year after year" (II Shmuel 21:1). Many people died and the distress grew. "And David sought the face of the Lord," that is, he inquired through the Urim and Tumim by means of the High Priest, for what they were being punished with famine. "And the Lord said: It is because of Shaul and because of his bloody house, because he put the Givonim to death." The Sages explained (Yerushalmi Sanhedrin 6:7; Radak and Malbim) that when Shaul was jealous of David and thought that the priests in the Mishkan of God at Nov were supporting David, he killed, together with the priests, seven Givonim as well. And although it was clear that the Givonim who were there had not taken part in the rebellion against him, Shaul killed them because he hated them for having deceived Israel in the days of Yehoshua, and he thought that since they had converted by deceit, it was fitting to persecute them and remove them from Israel. As it is stated: "And Shaul sought to slay them in his zeal for the children of Israel and Yehuda" (II Shmuel 21:2). In addition, following the killing of the priests at Nov, the livelihood of the Givonim, who supplied water and food to the Mishkan of God, ceased. And it seems that since everyone knew of King Shaul's hostile attitude toward the Givonim, the Givonim did not find another livelihood, and many of Israel began to persecute them until they were almost destroyed.

"And David said to the Givonim: What shall I do for you? And with what shall I make atonement, that you may bless the inheritance of the Lord? And the Givonim said to him: We will have no silver or gold of Shaul or of his house… The man who consumed us and who devised against us that we should be destroyed from remaining in any of the borders of Israel – let seven men of his sons be given to us, and we will hang them up to the Lord in Givat Shaul" (II Shmuel 21:3-6). David tried to persuade them to forgive the house of Shaul and to be appeased with a large monetary compensation, but they insisted and would not agree to forgive Israel unless they were given seven of Shaul's descendants to execute. Since David had been told through the Urim and Tumim that only after the Givonim forgave Israel would the famine cease, David was compelled to accept their demand. The king took two sons of Shaul and another five of his grandsons, "and he delivered them into the hands of the Givonim, and they hanged them on the mountain before the Lord, and the seven of them fell together." And they remained hanging on the tree throughout the whole summer.

The Sages asked (Yevamot 79a): But the halakha is that sons are not put to death for the sin of fathers! And they answered: "It is better that one letter be uprooted from the Torah, than that the name of Heaven be publicly desecrated." For had the sons of Shaul not been punished, the members of the nations of the world would have said: it is not fitting to cleave to this nation, which harms the converts who join it. They further asked: But the halakha is that those hanged on a tree are not left overnight; rather, one must take them down from the tree and bury them the same day, so how did they leave them hanging all summer? They answered: "It is better that one letter be uprooted from the Torah, and the name of Heaven be publicly sanctified." For the passers-by would say: What is the nature of these who are hanged? And they would answer them: "They are sons of kings!" They asked: And what did they do that they were punished so? They answered: "They laid their hands on gerim gerurim (converts who were dragged in)." The passers-by were amazed and said: "There is no nation as worthy of cleaving to as this one!" For if even sons of kings are punished like this for harming gerim gerurim, whose conversion was after the fact and by deceit, how much more so are they careful with the honour of righteous converts. "Immediately one hundred and fifty thousand were added to Israel," as it is stated (II Divrei Ha-yamim 2:16-17): "And Shlomo counted all the strangers who were in the land of Israel, after the census with which David his father had counted them, and they were found to be one hundred and fifty thousand… And he made seventy thousand of them bearers of burdens, and eighty thousand hewers in the mountain." And about this the Sages said (Yerushalmi Kiddushin 4:1): "Sanctification of the Name is greater than desecration of the Name."6

notes_en.en: The episode of the hanging of Shaul's sons by the Givonim appears in II Shmuel 21:1-14 and Bamidbar Rabba 8:4. I have explained the story by combining the words of the Sages and the commentators. Let us elaborate a little: In the Yerushalmi Kiddushin 4:1 and Sanhedrin 6:7, it is explained that Shaul killed seven of the Givonim: "two hewers of wood and two drawers of water, and a ḥazan, a scribe and an attendant." In the Bavli, Yevamot 78b, they objected that it is not stated in the Prophets that Shaul killed Givonim; therefore they explained that the complaint was that he deprived them of their livelihood. And it is possible that according to the Bavli those seven were killed together with the priests on the pretext that they were rebels against the kingdom, and therefore the Givonim could not complain about this; rather, they claimed against Shaul that he persecuted them, and as a result all of Israel took part in persecuting them until they were almost destroyed from the borders of Israel, and therefore all of Israel was punished with three years of famine. And although sons are not put to death for the sin of fathers, if the sons continued in their father's ways, they are punished. And here, although years had passed, Shaul's sons did not repent and even continued their hostile behaviour toward the Givonim (based on Radak, Abarbanel, Metzudot and Malbim. And Rav Sa'adya Gaon, cited in Radak, even explained that those seven who were hanged actually took part in killing them). In the commentary Mishmerot Kehuna on Yevamot 78b, he explained that as a result of Shaul's attitude toward the Givonim, many converts reverted to their former ways, and because of Israel's responsibility for this, they were punished with famine; and after they killed seven of Shaul's descendants, the converts returned to the good path. And although as a rule converts were not accepted in the days of David and Shlomo, these were accepted, for they were considered like apostate Jews who returned to their origin.

sections.title_en: Determining the Status of the Givonim
sections.body_en:
In the wake of the cruelty of the Givonim, who would not agree to be appeased with ransom and demanded the execution of seven of Shaul's descendants, David established that the prohibition to marry Givonim would remain for all generations. "He said: There are three signs in this nation: they are compassionate, bashful, and performers of kindness… Whoever has these three signs – is fit to cleave to this nation." And since they had no compassion for Shaul's descendants, he decreed that they may never marry them (Yevamot 79a). That is to say, although their conversion was valid, the Sages forbade marrying them (Mishna Yevamot 78b; SA EH 4:1).

Nevertheless, the Givonim remained connected to Israel, and together with them they went down into the Babylonian exile, and together with them they came up from Babylonia in the days of the building of the Second Temple, and they were called "Netinim" (Kiddushin 69a). In the days of Rabbi Yehuda Ha-nasi, more than a hundred years after the destruction of the Second Temple, they sought to abolish the subjugation of the Netinim in order to permit them to marry Israelites. Rabbi Yehuda Ha-nasi answered that although Israel can waive the subjugation to the service of the public, they cannot release the subjugation to the service of the altar. And so their law remained: they are Jews, but they are permitted to marry only among themselves and not with Israelites (Yevamot 79b). However, since the prohibition is rabbinic, after the fact (be-di'avad), if they transgressed and married, the marriage is valid and they are not required to divorce (see Rabbi Akiva Eiger, Ketubot 29a). And it seems that in this way many Givonim joined Israel, to the point that there was even a prophet among their descendants. On the other hand, there were other Givonim who after the destruction of the Second Temple went back and were assimilated among the gentiles.7

notes_en.en: Pesikta de-Rav Kahana 13: "Uriya – Israel would disparage him and say: Is he not a Givonite? 'And there was also a man who prophesied in the name of the Lord, Uriyahu son of Shemaya of Kiryat Ye'arim' (Yirmeyahu 26:20), and it is written: 'Now their cities were Givon, and Kefira, and Be'erot, and Kiryat Ye'arim' (Yehoshua 9:17); and Scripture needed to establish his lineage: 'And I will take for Me faithful witnesses, Uriya the priest' (Yeshayahu 8:2)." And likewise in Yalkut Shimoni, Pinḥas, remez 771, and Yirmeyahu 257. And the explanation is that Uriya was a priest, and they disparaged him for being a Givonite, for on his mother's side he was of their descendants, since according to halakha, if they transgressed and married, the marriage is valid. Apparently, in this way over the generations many of the descendants of the Givonim chose the Jewish identity and became part of Israel (see Kiddushin 72b, and Masoret Ha-giyur 16:11). On the other hand, since they converted through deceit, some of them retained a Givonite identity, and people did not marry them. And even if they intermingled with Israel, people tried to avoid marrying those in whom the cruel Givonite identity was evident, as the Rambam wrote (Hilkhot Issurei Bi'ah 19:17): "And so too, anyone who has brazenness or cruelty and hates people and does not perform kindness for them – one is very concerned about him lest he be a Givonite." Thus it happened that over time and through the exiles after the destruction of the Second Temple, many of the Givonim were assimilated among the gentiles and their name was lost, and there is no longer any hope that they will return, for the Sages said: "Even in the future to come the Holy One, blessed be He, will distance them" (Bamidbar Rabba 8:4; Yerushalmi Sanhedrin 6:7).

sections.body_en:
The policy of the Assyrian empire was to exile the peoples it conquered from their land to another land, so that they would be uprooted from their roots and subdued, and thus would engage in their work and pay heavy taxes and not organise to rebel. And so they did in the days of the First Temple to the Ten Tribes, whom, because of their sin, God gave into the hands of Assyria, and they exiled them to other provinces under their rule, and brought in their place members of other peoples "from Babylon, and from Kuta, and from Avva, and from Ḥamat, and Sefarvayim, and placed them in the cities of Shomron instead of the children of Israel; and they possessed Shomron and dwelt in its cities. And so it was at the beginning of their dwelling there, that they did not fear the Lord; therefore the Lord sent lions among them, which killed some of them. And they spoke to the king of Assyria, saying: The nations which you have exiled and placed in the cities of Shomron do not know the manner of the God of the land; therefore He has sent lions among them, and behold, they are killing them, because they do not know the manner of the God of the land. Then the king of Assyria commanded, saying: Take there one of the priests whom you exiled from there, and let them go and dwell there, and let him teach them the manner of the God of the land. So one of the priests whom they had exiled from Shomron came and dwelt in Beit El, and taught them how they should fear the Lord." But in practice, although they began to serve God, they did not abandon their idols; rather, "they feared the Lord, and served their own gods" (II Melakhim 17:24-28; 33).

Since most of the people who were exiled to Shomron came from Kuta, they were all called after them "Kutim." Later they were called "Shomronim" (Samaritans), after their place of residence in Shomron. For about one hundred and thirty years the Kutim lived in Shomron while the First Temple in Jerusalem still stood on its site, and some of them went up to it on pilgrimage. As is told in the Prophets (Yirmeyahu 41:5) about pilgrims from Shomron who, in the middle of their way to the Temple, learned that it had been destroyed, as it is stated: "There came men from Shekhem, from Shilo and from Shomron, eighty men, having their beards shaven and their clothes torn and having cut themselves, with meal-offerings and frankincense in their hand to bring to the House of the Lord." However, it is possible that those going up to the Temple were Israelites who remained in Shomron, for it is reasonable that even after the kingdom of Assyria exiled the Ten Tribes, many Israelites still remained in small villages. And it seems more likely that the Kutim intermingled and intermarried with the Israelites and priests who remained scattered in Shomron, and over time all of them together were considered Kutim, and some of them went up to the First Temple until it was destroyed by the kingdom of Babylon.

The Tanna'im disagreed whether according to halakha the Kutim have the status of Jews or of gentiles (Kiddushin 75b). In the opinion of Rabbi Yishmael they have the status of gentiles, because at the time of their conversion they did not abandon their idols and continued to practise idolatry. However, in the opinion of Rabbi Akiva and most of the Sages they have the status of Jews, and although after their conversion they continued to worship idols, since they converted and accepted upon themselves that God is the God of gods, their conversion is valid. And some explain that at first they were not considered Jews, because at the time of the conversion they intended to continue practising idolatry, but when they abandoned their idols and began to serve God, they converted again and became Jews. And so Israel was accustomed for many generations to regard them as Jews.8

notes_en.en: In several places it is stated in the Mishna anonymously that the Kutim are considered true converts (Berakhot 45a; Ketubot 29a; Nedarim 31a, and more), and this is also the opinion of several Amora'im: Rabbi Yoḥanan, Rabbi Abahu, Rabbi Ami, Rabbi Asi, Rabbi Zeira, Abaye and Rava (Ḥullin 3-6). And so the Rambam wrote as halakha (Hilkhot Avadim 6:6), and so wrote many Rishonim, because even when the conversion is done out of fear of lions it is valid, and the fact that they continued to practise idolatry caused them to be considered apostate Israelites (Rashba and Ritva on Yevamot 24b; Rambam, Commentary on the Mishna, Berakhot 8:8). And according to those who hold that their conversion is not valid, the Ramban explained (Kiddushin 75b, s.v. "de-amar") that this is because at the time of their conversion they continued to practise idolatry, "and the name of idol worship was never forgotten from their mouths, nor its worship from their hands." And Tosafot (Yevamot 24b, s.v. "halakha") explained that the view of those who hold that they are not converts is because they continued to practise idolatry, and those who hold that they are converts agree that at first their conversion was not valid, because they continued to practise idolatry, but afterward they converted again completely. And so wrote Tosafot in other places (Sukka 8b, s.v. "sukkat"; Ḥullin 3b, s.v. "ka-savar"; and so wrote Tosafot Ha-Rosh there). (See Masoret Ha-giyur 7:22.)

sections.body_en:
When the exiles of Babylonia began to go up to Jerusalem toward the building of the Second Temple, a deep hostility developed between them and the Kutim, to the point that the Kutim were called "the adversaries of Yehuda and Binyamin." And when Zerubavel son of She'altiel, the political leader, and Yeshua son of Yotzadak, the High Priest, began to build the Temple, the adversaries of Yehuda approached them "and said to them: Let us build with you (the Temple), for we seek your God as you do, and we have been sacrificing to Him since the days of Esar-ḥaddon king of Assyria, who brought us up here. But Zerubavel and Yeshua and the rest of the heads of the fathers' houses of Israel said to them: You have nothing to do with us in building a house to our God, but we ourselves together will build to the Lord, the God of Israel, as King Koresh, the king of Persia, has commanded us" (Ezra 4:2-3). The commentators explained that the leaders of those who had come up knew that the Kutim wanted to participate in the building of the Temple with the aim of preventing its construction, and therefore they refused to include them in building it (Rashi and Metzudot). And it is possible that at that time the Kutim had already begun to establish their religious centre on Mount Gerizim, and wanted to participate in the Temple as well, and to this they could not agree, for the Temple in Jerusalem must be the one and only place for the service of God. And it is possible that they also knew that the Kutim were still practising idolatry in partnership (with the service of God), and feared that with their idolatrous stance they would corrupt the Temple service (see Malbim there).

Great tension arose between those who had come up to Yehuda and the Kutim, and the adversaries of Yehuda sent letters of accusation to the king of Persia against the Jews, and caused the building of the Temple to be delayed for eighteen years (Ezra 4:5-24; Rashi there 24). Meanwhile, religious differences developed between those who had come up to Yehuda and the Kutim. In Yehuda, by decision of Ezra and the Men of the Great Assembly, they switched to the Assyrian script, whereas the Kutim remained with the ancient Hebrew script (Sanhedrin 21b). The Kutim built themselves a temple on Mount Gerizim and falsified the Torah, writing explicitly that the place God chose for His Temple is Mount Gerizim. The Kutim also did not accept the enactments of the Sages, and conducted themselves according to their own understanding of Scripture. The tension reached a point where the Kutim asked the Greeks to destroy the Temple (Yoma 69a; Megillat Ta'anit 9). Later, when the Hasmoneans prevailed, Yoḥanan Hyrcanus conquered the region of Shomron and destroyed the temple of the Samaritans.

And still, in the opinion of most of the Sages, from a halakhic standpoint the Kutim were considered Jews, and it was permitted to marry them. And they even said that every mitzva that the Kutim are careful about, they are more meticulous in it than Israel (Kiddushin 76a).

However, the tension between the Jews and the Kutim grew greater and greater, especially in the days of the destruction of the Temple and the Bar Kokhba revolt, when the Kutim joined the enemies of Israel. At the same time, the distance in the manner of observing the mitzvot grew, until in the days of the Amora Rabbi Abahu, when it became clear that there were no longer any among the Kutim who observed the Torah properly, and they even found the image of a dove at the top of Mount Gerizim which they would worship, the Sages decreed regarding the Kutim that they be considered gentiles (Ḥullin 6a). And the Sages said (Tractate Kutim 2:8) that they can be accepted back into Judaism "once they renounce Mount Gerizim and acknowledge Jerusalem and the resurrection of the dead," that is, the redemption of Israel. Afterward they will convert and once again be like Jews in every respect.9

notes_en.en: Ḥullin 6a: "They made them complete idol worshippers." Some say that they are considered gentiles, and their betrothals (kiddushin) are not valid betrothals (Rambam, Hilkhot Avadim 6:6; Meiri, Nedarim 31a; Shakh YD 159:5). And some say that since they only decreed that they be considered gentiles, by Torah law their status is that of Jews, and therefore if there was a betrothal between a Jew and a Kutit (Samaritan woman) or vice versa – the betrothal is valid, and they must separate and arrange a get (bill of divorce) out of doubt (Behag, end of Hilkhot Kiddushin; Tur and SA EH 44:10; Gra 19; see Piskei Din Rabbaniyim 14, p. 89, in the words of Rav Shlomo Dichovsky and Rav Avraham Elkana Shapira). However, for other matters the decree that they be considered gentiles stands in place (Ḥatam Sofer, Ḥullin 5b; Arukh La-ner, Nidda 57a). And they are accepted back into Judaism as cited in Tractate Kutim 2:8: "once they renounce Mount Gerizim and acknowledge Jerusalem and the resurrection of the dead," that is, they believe in the redemption of Israel. And then they must convert "in the manner that gentiles must convert" (Riaz, Gittin 1:2:10). And although they are doubtfully Jews, and because of this some are concerned about mamzerut regarding them (Tur; Beit Shmuel EH 4:63), in practice there is no concern about mamzerut, since a doubt in a rabbinic matter is resolved leniently (Atzei Arazim EH 4:66; and so wrote Rav Shapira in Piskei Din Rabbaniyim there).

sections.title_en: The Distancing of the Foreign Wives in the Days of Ezra
sections.body_en:
At the beginning of the days of the Second Temple, a generation after the beginning of the ascent of the returnees from Babylonia led by Zerubavel toward the building of the Second Temple, Ezra the Scribe received authority from the king of Persia to enforce religious matters in Jerusalem and Yehuda, and he went up to Jerusalem at the head of a group of returnees. A short time after his arrival in the Land, some of the officers of the people raised before him the grave problem of intermarriage among the returnees to Zion, and said: "The people of Israel, and the priests and the Levites, have not separated themselves from the peoples of the lands, doing according to their abominations, of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Jebusites, the Ammonites, the Moabites, the Egyptians and the Amorites. For they have taken of their daughters for themselves and for their sons, so that the holy seed has mingled itself with the peoples of the lands; and the hand of the officers and rulers has been first in this trespass" (Ezra 9:1-2). Ezra knew that intermarriage could lead to betrayal of God and His Torah and to following idols, and thereby cause another destruction of the Jewish settlement that had begun to develop in Jerusalem and Yehuda. Therefore: "And when I heard this thing, I tore my garment and my robe, and plucked out the hair of my head and of my beard, and sat appalled. Then there were gathered to me everyone who trembled at the words of the God of Israel because of the trespass of the exiles, and I sat appalled until the evening offering. And at the evening offering I arose from my fasting, with my garment and my robe torn, and I fell upon my knees and spread out my hands to the Lord my God" (ibid. 9:3-5). In the course of his prayer he confessed the sin of the people: "And now, O our God, what shall we say after this? For we have forsaken Your commandments" (ibid. 10). For God commanded: "Do not give your daughters to their sons, nor take their daughters for your sons, nor seek their peace or their prosperity forever, that you may be strong and eat the good of the land, and leave it as an inheritance to your children forever. And after all that has come upon us for our evil deeds and for our great guilt," if we again break His commandment by marrying idol worshippers, "would You not be angry with us until You had consumed us, so that there would be no remnant nor any to escape?" (ibid. 12-14).

While Ezra was praying and confessing before God, a great congregation of Israel gathered to him, and they wept over their situation. Shekhanya son of Yeḥiel responded and said to Ezra: indeed we have sinned, but it is possible to rectify it. "Now therefore let us make a covenant with our God to put away all the wives and those born of them, according to the counsel of my lord and of those who tremble at the commandment of our God, and let it be done according to the Torah. Arise, for the matter is upon you, and we are with you; be strong and do it." It was decided to gather all the returnees from exile to Jerusalem on the 20th of Kislev, and whoever did not come – his property would be confiscated and he would be separated from the congregation. At the assembly, which took place in the cold and the rain, Ezra repeated his rebuke and called upon those gathered to separate themselves "from the peoples of the land and from the foreign wives. Then all the congregation answered and said with a loud voice: As you have said, so must we do" (Ezra 10:1-12). However, since the matter required detailed handling, "for we have greatly transgressed in this matter," it was established that the officers and elders would stand and examine who had sinned by marrying foreign wives, and would oversee the separation from them. In the process of examination, which lasted three months, it became clear that even prominent priests had sinned in this, among them also the sons of Yehoshua son of Yehotzadak the High Priest (ibid. 13-18). As the prophet Zekharya saw in his vision (3:3): "Now Yehoshua was clothed in filthy garments, and was standing before the angel." His filthy garments were the sins of his sons who had married foreign wives (Sanhedrin 93a; Radak, Zekharya 3:3). On the 1st of Nisan they completed the separation of the Jews from the foreign wives, and it was found that one hundred and thirteen Jews divorced their foreign wives, and those who had also borne children – were sent away with their children (Ezra 10:20-44).

It must be added that, in addition to the sin of intermarriage, there was also a terrible betrayal by the returnees from Babylonia of their wives. As it is stated (Malakhi 2:11-16): "Yehuda has dealt treacherously, and an abomination has been committed in Israel and in Jerusalem; for Yehuda has profaned the holiness of the Lord which He loves, and has married the daughter of a foreign god. May the Lord cut off from the man who does this him who wakes and him who answers, out of the tents of Yaakov, and him who offers an offering to the Lord of hosts… Because the Lord has been witness between you and the wife of your youth, against whom you have dealt treacherously, though she is your companion and the wife of your covenant… Therefore take heed to your spirit, and let none deal treacherously against the wife of his youth. For I hate sending away, says the Lord, the God of Israel, and covering one's garment with violence, says the Lord of hosts (God hates one who sends away the wife of his youth and supports another in her place); therefore take heed to your spirit, that you do not deal treacherously." The Sages said (Megilla 15a) that Malakhi is Ezra. His name as head of the Sanhedrin was Ezra, and his prophetic name was Malakhi. As head of the Sanhedrin he acted to send away the foreign wives, and as a prophet he prophesied about the betrayal by the returnees from Babylonia of their wives, who had come up with them faithfully. And so the Sages said: "When Israel came up from the exile, the faces of the women were blackened by the sun (because of the hardships of the journey), and they left them and went and married Ammonite women, and (their abandoned wives) would surround the altar and weep." That is what Malakhi says (2:13): "And this further you do: you cover the altar of the Lord with tears, with weeping and with sighing." A betrayal of this kind happened the first time at Shittim with the daughters of Midyan, and now they returned a second time to betray their wives with young foreign women and to abandon them without a livelihood. And about this they said: "After you have robbed and wronged her and taken her beauty from her, you send her away?!" (Bereshit Rabba 18:5. And so explained Rashi, Radak and Metzudot on Malakhi 2:13-16).

sections.title_en: The Sending Away of the Wives in the Days of Neḥemya
sections.body_en:
About thirteen years later, Neḥemya went up to the Land and needed to act once again to separate the Jews from intermarriage. Apparently, despite the great awakening to repentance, many of Israel still remained in mixed marriages, and in the meantime more Jews who had married foreign women were added to them. Neḥemya held governmental authority of the highest rank. At first he was the cupbearer of the king of Persia, and since he yearned to take part in building the Land, he received permission from the king of Persia to go up to Yehuda and to rule on his behalf over the "province of Yehuda." Immediately after his ascent he harnessed everyone to building the walls of Jerusalem, and stabilised the status of the poor who had been exploited by the rich. Thereby he strengthened Yehuda in terms of security, society and economy (Neḥemya 1-6). Afterward he assembled the people to celebrate Rosh Ha-shana at the Temple, and Ezra the Scribe read from the Torah scroll, and the people were aroused with weeping to repent. But Ezra and Neḥemya postponed the assembly of repentance until after Sukkot, and in the meantime encouraged the people to rejoice in the festivals of Tishrei. "Now on the twenty-fourth day of this month the children of Israel were assembled with fasting, and with sackcloth, and earth upon them. And the seed of Israel separated themselves from all foreigners, and stood and confessed their sins and the iniquities of their fathers" (Neḥemya 9:1-2).10

After twelve years of his rule in Jerusalem, Neḥemya had to return to the palace of the king of Persia. After he stayed there for a certain period, he received permission to return to Jerusalem and to rule it. When he returned he found once again that there were many Jews who had married gentiles, and their children were growing up as complete foreigners. As it is stated (Neḥemya 13:23-27): "In those days also I saw the Jews who had married women of Ashdod, of Ammon and of Moav. And their children spoke half in the speech of Ashdod, and could not speak in the language of the Jews, but according to the language of each people." Since the king of Persia had granted him governmental powers in order to enforce the laws of the kingdom and the religion of Israel, this is what he did: "And I contended with them, and cursed them, and struck some of them, and plucked off their hair, and made them swear by God: You shall not give your daughters to their sons, nor take their daughters for your sons or for yourselves. Did not Shlomo king of Israel sin by these things? Yet among many nations there was no king like him, and he was beloved of his God, and God made him king over all Israel – even him did the foreign women cause to sin. Shall we then listen to you to do all this great evil, to trespass against our God in marrying foreign women?!" In summing up his words he related that he chased away those who profaned the priesthood by marrying foreign women, and established the watches of the priests and the Levites. And regarding Israel – "Thus I cleansed them from everything foreign… Remember me, O my God, for good." With this the books of Ezra and Neḥemya conclude.

notes_en.en: The story of the reading of the Torah and the making of the covenant appears in the book of Neḥemya, chapters 8-10, and the implication is that they took place in the days of Neḥemya's rule as governor of Yehuda. However, some say that it took place mainly in the days of Zerubavel, at the beginning of the Return to Zion, and it is mentioned in the book of Neḥemya because at that time, together with Ezra, he renewed that same covenant (see Peninei Halakha, Kashrut 12:7). In any case, from the fact that Neḥemya chose to bring this story as part of the description of his deeds during the period of his rule in Yehuda, we learn that when he went up to the Land, in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes king of Persia, thirteen years after the sending away of the foreign wives under the leadership of Ezra, he again encountered the problem of marriage to foreign women and was required to deal with it. And so it happened also in the period of his second rule, after he received further authorisation from the king of Persia to return to the Land.

sections.title_en: Why They Did Not Try to Convert the Foreign Wives
sections.body_en:
Although the sending away of the wives and children surely caused great sorrow, both to the wives and children and to the men, we do not find that they tried to convert the wives, because the halakha is that conversion must be for the sake of Heaven and not for the sake of marriage. And had they offered them to convert, it would have been clear that their conversion was for the sake of marriage. And although after the fact, if they converted a convert for the sake of marriage, his conversion is a valid conversion (Yevamot 24b; below 4:4), one may be lenient in this only in a pressing situation (she'at ha-deḥak), when the convert intends to live as a Jew. However, the identity of those women was foreign, and they did not want to change it, for they remained living near the members of their families, who were of the peoples who had invaded the Land following the destruction. This was expressed in the fact that many of their children "could not speak in the language of the Jews," but spoke the language of their mothers' families. In addition, the national and spiritual status of the Jews in Yehuda was shaky, and there was a concern that if converts who did not identify with Judaism joined them, the enterprise of the returnees to Zion would go to ruin. Therefore they did not try to convert the foreign wives but instructed that they be sent away.

In the wake of the activity of Ezra and Neḥemya, many sent away their foreign wives, but not all sent away their wives, and perhaps some pretended to send them away and then took them back again. As is proven by the fact that thirteen years after the covenant they made with Ezra to send away the wives, Neḥemya needed to act again to abolish the mixed marriages. And thirteen years later, when he returned a second time to rule over Yehuda, he needed to act against them with greater severity.

Apparently, many of the foreign wives did not want to convert, because they were attached to the members of their families and to their foreign identity. Therefore, every time their sending away was spoken of, they returned with their children to their foreign family, and after a time, when the pressure weakened, they returned to their Jewish husbands but remained attached to their family and their foreign identity, to the point that their children did not know how to speak the language of the Jews. Not only that, but at times their father and their Jewish spouse harmed the building of Jerusalem (Neḥemya 2:19; 13:7), and perhaps they even served as spies against Israel (Neḥemya 6:17-19). And therefore Ezra and Neḥemya needed to act again and again to send them away.

It is also reasonable that there were foreign women who preferred to remain with their Jewish husbands. And although in principle they should have been sent away, for one does not convert for the sake of marriage, since after the fact a conversion for the sake of marriage is valid, families who wanted to convert the women found a way to convert them. And after they converted, Ezra and Neḥemya did not demand that they be sent away. However, since many of them continued to practise idolatry and to conduct a foreign way of life, Ezra and Neḥemya needed to act again to send them away. However, those who conducted themselves as Jewish women were accepted into Israel even though they had not converted for the sake of Heaven (see the note).11

notes_en.en:
Some hold that they did not convert even one of the foreign wives, for one does not convert for the sake of marriage (Pekudat Elazar YD 116; Kiryat Ḥana David, vol. 2, YD 17). And some say that they instructed that all of them be sent away in order to fence in the generation as a temporary measure (Rav Shalom Kutna in Ve-khatora Ye'aseh; Rav Ḥayim David Halevi in Aseh Lekha Rav 3:29). And some explained that they were from the seven nations whom it is forbidden to marry (one explanation by Rav Kalischer, Mishnat Avraham on the Semag, negative commandment 116). And Rav Yosef Mashash added a reason for sending them away: that by marrying them they betrayed the Jewish wives (Otzar Ha-mikhtavim 2:859), as cited in section 11.
However, on the other hand, in the opinion of many, women who wished could have converted, as Rav Refael Birdugo wrote (Mesamḥei Lev on Ezra 9), that the foreign wives who were sent away in the days of Ezra did not want to convert, but had they wanted to, Ezra and his court would have converted them. And so wrote, as one of the possibilities, Rav Kalischer, and Rav Uziel (Piskei Uziel bi-She'elot Ha-zeman 64). See Masoret Ha-giyur 6:2-8. As explained above, from the fact that they needed to fence in the public three times, it follows that in practice not everyone sent away his wife. Moreover, from the fact that it was emphasised that the women raised their children as gentiles and their sons did not know how to speak the language of the Jews, one can learn that had they raised their children as Jews there would not have been a severe demand to send them away. Therefore we are compelled to conclude that some of the women converted, and they were the ones who raised their children as Jews. Similarly, Rav Yissakhar Tamar wrote that in practice most of the women converted, and they sent away only those who continued to practise idolatry (Alei Tamar, Kiddushin 3:12, s.v. "ve-khatora"; Masoret Ha-giyur 6:9).

sections.body_en:
In the days of Yoḥanan Hyrcanus, the Hasmonean priest, the tribes of the Edomites were converted and attached themselves to Israel. The place of residence of the Edomites was in the mountains of Edom south of the Dead Sea, but after the destruction of the First Temple they invaded the territory of Yehuda and settled in various cities in the region of the Hebron hills and the Judean lowlands (Shefela). Their large cities were Adoraim and Maresha. Apparently the number of converts was several tens of thousands. Regarding their conversion, Josephus (Yosef ben Matityahu) related (in Antiquities of the Jews) that Yoḥanan the Priest conquered the cities of the Edomites and put a choice before them: to convert through circumcision and undertake to observe the mitzvot of the Torah, or to leave their land. The Edomites chose to convert. He also related that Yoḥanan's successors converted in a similar manner the tribes of the Itureans who lived in the Lebanon valley and the northern Golan.

Yoḥanan the Priest, who converted them, was the grandson of Matityahu the Priest, who raised the banner of revolt against the Greeks, who had defiled the Temple and forced Israel to transgress their religion. Thanks to the victories of Matityahu's sons under the leadership of Yehuda the Maccabee, the Temple was liberated and purified (3596 from the creation of the world), and in memory of this we celebrate Ḥanukka to this day. Afterward the Greeks returned with large forces, and Yehuda was killed in battle against them. His brother Yonatan continued to lead Israel for ten years, until he was killed by trickery by the Greeks. His brother Shimon led Israel after him for seven years, until he too was killed in a treacherous revolt that the Greeks organised against him. At this difficult hour, Yoḥanan, the son of Shimon, began to lead Israel for thirty-one years. Through a combination of diplomacy and military valour, he succeeded in strengthening Yehuda and expanding its borders, from the areas surrounding Jerusalem to all of Yehuda and most of Shomron (see Peninei Halakha, Zemanim 11:3-4, note 3).

In addition to being the Nasi (leader) of Yehuda, Yoḥanan also served as High Priest, and the Sages said that he even merited divine inspiration (ru'aḥ ha-kodesh). Once, when he entered the Holy of Holies on Yom Kippur, he heard a heavenly voice (bat kol) proclaiming that his army had defeated the Greeks at Antioch, and they wrote down that hour and it became clear that indeed at that very hour Israel had defeated their enemies (Sota 33a). Yoḥanan also strengthened the people in the observance of the mitzvot, and enacted important halakhic enactments (Mishna Ma'aser Sheni 5:15). But in his old age he was drawn after the Sadducees, and about him the Sages said: "Do not trust in yourself until the day of your death, for Yoḥanan the High Priest served in the High Priesthood for eighty years, and in the end became a Sadducee" (Berakhot 29a). After all this, his days were considered the best days of the rule of the Hasmonean house, days in which Israel was faithful to the Torah and the mitzvot, and merited military and political success and economic prosperity.

But it is difficult: conversion must be personal and with full consent, so how could Yoḥanan, who was a Torah scholar, a tzaddik and possessed of divine inspiration, convert the Edomites as an entire group and by coercion? Some say that indeed the conversion of the Edomites was done improperly under the influence of the positions of the Sadducees, and its results were negative, for from those converts came Herod, who seized the Hasmonean kingdom and killed the Sages, and became known for his wickedness and cruelty (Rav Yitzḥak Isaac Halevi, author of Dorot Ha-rishonim).

And some say that the Edomites were not converted to be Jews, but rather were subjugated as slaves, and their conversion was for the purpose of slavery, and accordingly was done under semi-coercion. And the proof of this is that the Sages said (Bava Batra 3b; Kiddushin 70b) that Herod, who seized the Hasmonean kingdom, was by law a slave (Rav Uziel).

And Rav Goren explained that Yoḥanan the Priest, who was righteous and wise, wanted to strengthen Yehuda and consolidate it, and relied on the fact that thanks to the Jewish majority that had taken shape in the Land of Israel, the Edomites would integrate into Israel and ultimately identify fully with the Torah of Israel. This position accords with what is explained in the Talmud Yerushalmi and in Tractate Gerim, that in the Land of Israel one should relate positively to conversion initiatives. In practice, the Edomites did integrate into Israel, and the Sages said that among their descendants were disciples in the House of Shammai; and in the days of the destruction of the Temple they fought with self-sacrifice against the Romans for the freedom of the people, the Temple and the Land of Israel. And even the kingdom of Herod, who was of the descendants of the Edomites, despite his wickedness, was considered a Jewish kingdom that benefited Israel. Therefore the Rambam (Hilkhot Ḥanukka 3:1) includes the days of his rule as well among the two hundred good years in which the kingship returned to Israel thanks to the victories of the Hasmoneans.12

notes_en.en: Among those who hold that their conversion was not proper: Rav Yitzḥak Isaac Halevi in Dorot Ha-rishonim 1:3, "The Sadducees," chapter 10. And likewise Rav Reuven Margaliot (Devarim Be-itam 8); Rav Yekutiel Yehuda Greenwald, Le-toldot Ha-sanhedrin Be-Yisrael 3, note 19; Ḥevel Naḥalato 9:33, and others. Among those who hold that the Edomites were not converted but subjugated as slaves: Rav Uziel, and in his opinion when a slave is captured in war it is not necessary that he agree to accept the mitzvot, and only when one buys a slave from a gentile is it necessary that he agree to accept the mitzvot (Derashot Uziel on Tractate Avot, p. 50). And in the opinion of Rav Pines, Yoḥanan erred, for according to halakha the slave must agree to accept the mitzvot (Li-Shlomo, p. 190). Rav Uziel further wrote that the Hasmoneans erred in giving the Edomites a place in Jerusalem, and as a result they succeeded in seizing their kingdom. The words of Rav Goren were cited in Shana Be-shana 5756, p. 174.
