The Ramban wrote (Sefer Ha-ge'ula 3) that among the Edomites were the first who erred after "that man," and from them the Christian faith spread to Rome, and therefore the Sages identify Rome with Edom. And so wrote Abarbanel (Yeshayahu 35).

sections.title_en: The Conversion of Male and Female Slaves
sections.body_en:
Until about two hundred years ago, for thousands of years, slavery was widespread throughout the world. People were certain that the institution of slavery was natural to human society, and that this was the proper way for humanity to exist in the relatively best manner. This is not the place to examine this, but we will note that the Torah does not try to uproot human nature but to elevate and refine it. For this purpose the laws of slaves were given, to guide Israel to act according to the highest possible moral standard even while they were compelled to maintain slavery, and in the process to establish principles that would mark the path to the abolition of slavery. This subject is connected to the laws of conversion, because the male and female slaves who were bought by Israelites had to agree to undergo conversion, as will be explained in this section, and if they were freed they would become full Jews, as explained in the next section.

An Israelite who bought male or female slaves from the members of the nations must make their purchase conditional on their agreeing to undergo conversion and to obligate themselves in the mitzvot in which slaves are obligated, that is, in all the mitzvot of the Torah, except for the mitzvot connected to the prohibitions of forbidden relations (arayot) and marital relations, in which their laws are different. In addition, slaves are exempt from time-bound positive mitzvot, from which even Jewish women are exempt (Ḥagiga 4a). Therefore slaves are obligated in mezuza and in the Pesaḥ offering, and exempt from tzitzit and tefillin. The general rule is: when the slaves convert, they leave the category of gentiles, but they have not yet reached the status of Israel (Rambam, Hilkhot Issurei Bi'ah 12:11). And such is the law of the descendants of a female slave until the end of all generations.

Therefore, when a person of Israel wished to buy a slave from the nations, he had to bring him before a court of three in order to convert him. And one does not ask him whether he wishes to join the people of Israel, for since he is a slave, he is drawn in this after his master. But with regard to the mitzvot, one must ask him whether he is prepared to accept them, and in the way that all converts are accepted, one informs him of the fundamentals of the religion and some of the lighter and more severe mitzvot and their punishment and reward (SA YD 267:3). If he agreed – it is a mitzva for his master to circumcise him, just as Avraham our father was commanded to circumcise his slaves (Bereshit 17:12-13), and the mohel recites a blessing on his circumcision (SA 267:1; 12). After he heals from the circumcision, he immerses before three, and while he is still in the water he accepts the mitzvot upon himself. Since the immersion is based on the slave's decision to convert and accept the mitzvot, it is the slave who recites the blessing on the immersion and not the master (SA and Rema 267:3). And such is the law of a female slave: she must be accepted in a court and immerse with a blessing for the sake of her conversion.

If at the time of their purchase the male or female slave was undecided whether they agreed to convert and accept the mitzvot, the master was permitted to keep them with him for up to twelve months, in the hope that he would succeed in educating them toward this and they would agree to convert and accept the mitzvot. If the twelve months passed and they did not agree – the master is obligated to sell them to a gentile (SA 267:4).13

After their conversion, the master is obligated to enable his male and female slaves to observe mitzvot; therefore he is forbidden to sell them to a gentile, for they will not be able to observe mitzvot properly with him. If he transgressed and sold them to a gentile, the Sages fined him that he must redeem them at a price of up to ten times their value, and afterward he is obligated to free them (Gittin 44a; SA 267:80).

Likewise, a master who lives in the Land of Israel is forbidden to compel his slave to go down with him outside the Land, for thereby he prevents him from the mitzva of settling the Land, and anyone who lives outside the Land is like one who practises idolatry (Ketubot 110b). And if the slave did not agree to go down with him, he is obligated to sell him to a master who lives in the Land or to free him (Gittin 43b; 44a; SA 267:82).

Moreover, a male or female slave who was bought outside the Land can demand of their master to go up to the Land in order to fulfil the mitzva of settling the Land, and then either the master goes up with them, or he sells them to a master who lives in the Land, or he frees them (Ketubot 110b; SA 267:84). And if the master did not agree, and the slave fled and went up to the Land, the Torah commanded not to return him to his master outside the Land, as it is stated (Devarim 23:16-17): "You shall not deliver to his master a slave who has escaped from his master to you. He shall dwell with you, in your midst, in the place which he shall choose within one of your gates, where it pleases him best; you shall not wrong him." Rather, the master must free him with a bill of manumission (get shiḥrur). And if he did not agree to free him, the court annuls his servitude and frees him (Gittin 45a; SA 267:85).14

notes_en.en:
According to the Rif, the Rambam and SA 267:5, "If he circumcised his slave and immersed him against his will for the sake of slavery – he has done nothing." (But with regard to rabbinic laws, such as yayin nesekh and bishul akum, his status is like that of a Jew – Radbaz 4:49; Pitḥei Teshuva 267:1.) And some disagree and hold that the master can circumcise and immerse the slave against his will, and thereby he becomes obligated in all the mitzvot of a slave, but the Sages instructed not to do so, because if the male or female slave does not identify with Judaism, they will cause their masters to stumble in matters of the forbidden and permitted (Rashi, Ramban and Nimukei Yosef).
At the time when the Jubilee was in force, in a case where the slave did not agree to accept the mitzvot upon himself, after the fact it was possible to suffice with his accepting upon himself before the court to be a ger toshav, that is, to keep the seven Noahide commandments out of belief in the Torah. However, since the Jubilees ceased, about one hundred and fifty years before the destruction of the First Temple, the court has no authority to accept a ger toshav (Rambam, Hilkhot Issurei Bi'ah 14:8-9). According to the Ra'avad, the authority that ceased from the court is to accept a ger toshav for the status in which one is obligated to sustain him, but it is possible to accept his undertaking to observe the seven Noahide commandments, and in this way to accept him into slavery. And so they practised in Ashkenaz (Rema 267:4). Such a slave does not become a Jew when he is freed. According to my teacher and master Rav Tzvi Yehuda Kook (notes to Mishpat Kohen, no. 63, p. 363), according to the Ra'avad it suffices for this purpose that he accept not to practise idolatry, and according to Rav Yisraeli (Amud Ha-yemini 12:15) acceptance of all seven Noahide commandments is required.

When a slave fled from outside the Land to the Land, and the master does not want to lose his slave, in the opinion of the Ritva (Gittin 45a) and the Ran (on the Rif, Gittin 23b), he may go up to the Land or sell him to a resident of the Land. And according to the Rambam (Hilkhot Avadim 8:9-11), if the master did not agree that the slave go up to the Land, and as a result the slave fled and went up, the master has lost his right to subjugate him, and he goes out to freedom, and his master is obligated to write him a bill of manumission. The Rosh (Gittin 4:43) has an intermediate opinion, according to which even if the master goes up to the Land he cannot go back to subjugating him, lest he persuade him to go back out of the Land, but he may sell him to another master who lives in the Land of Israel.
The commentators explained regarding the verse "You shall not deliver to his master a slave who has escaped from his master to you" (Devarim 23:16), that the plain meaning of the verse deals with a gentile slave who fled from his gentile master in order to cleave to the faith of Israel and to serve God, and therefore he should not be rejected after he has trusted in us and come to take shelter under the wings of the Shekhina (Targum Yonatan, Onkelos, Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Ramban, and others). And the Meiri wrote (Gittin 45a) that this explanation too is correct as halakha, and so wrote the Ḥatam Sofer there.

sections.title_en: Upon Being Freed, Slaves Become Jews
sections.body_en:
When a male or female slave is freed, they become Jews in every respect. For upon entering servitude they converted, and thereby they and their descendants entered into an eternal covenant with God and with His people Israel. But as long as they are slaves, they are not obligated in all the mitzvot, and when they are freed they become obligated in all the mitzvot like all of Israel. Even when the male or female slave wanted to remain slaves, if the master freed them – against their will they become free Jews, and they can no longer go back to being gentiles (Rema 267:5). However, the Sages required them to immerse after their release before three for the sake of full entry into Israel, but they do not need to obligate themselves in the mitzvot again (SA 267:7; and see Rabbi Akiva Eiger there).

Over time all the male and female slaves were freed, and according to the halakha they became full Jews. However, when Israel was defeated, their slaves passed into the possession of the victors, and presumably they also forced them to accept their religion, and thereby they were lost from Israel. But when the release was done within Israel, the slaves became Jews, and thus many converts joined Israel15

A slave is freed in three ways: 1) by a document, 2) by money, 3) when the master injured one of his chief limbs (SA 267:26).

The first way: the master can free his slave by means of a "bill of manumission," in which it is written that he frees him to freedom, and he hands him the document before two witnesses, and thereby the slave is freed (SA 267:41; 44).

The second way: another person can pay the master the sum required for the slave's release, and when the master receives the money the release takes effect (Kiddushin 22b; SA 267:26).

The third way: if the master injured one of the slave's chief limbs with an injury that does not heal – he goes out to freedom, and the master is compelled to write him a bill of manumission. For example, if he blinded his eye or deafened his ear, or caused one of his fingertips to be cut off, or injured one of his limbs in a way that it cannot function, or even knocked out one of his teeth (SA 267:27-35; 40). It is worth noting that in ancient times it was customary to mark male and female slaves by removing two front teeth from their mouths or cutting their ear or one of their fingers, and according to halakha, if the master did this to his slave, he goes out to freedom.16

notes_en.en: It is stated regarding a Canaanite slave (Vayikra 25:46): "And you shall bequeath them to your children after you, to inherit as a possession; you shall make them serve you forever," and such is the law of a slave from all the other nations as well. It is explained in Gittin 38b that according to Rabbi Yishmael this is an optional mitzva, that is, it is permitted to continue to subjugate them forever, but if the master wishes to free them – he may. And according to Rabbi Akiva this is an obligatory mitzva, so that one who frees his slave – nullifies a positive commandment. And the halakha follows Rabbi Akiva. However, in order to fulfil a mitzva, even a rabbinic one, it is permitted to free a slave, as Rabbi Eliezer freed his slave in order to complete a minyan (Berakhot 47b; SA 267:79). Seemingly this is difficult: how can a rabbinic mitzva override a mitzva from the Torah? The Rishonim explained that the prohibition to free a slave is only because of the prohibition of "lo teḥonem," not to give him a free gift. But when the Israelite wants this for himself or for another reason, even if there is no great need for it, this is not a "free gift" and it is permitted (Ramban and Ran, Gittin there). Therefore, if a person said at the time of his death: "My maidservant – let them not subjugate her," the heirs are compelled to free her (Gittin 40a). And they have no prohibition in this, for presumably he commanded this on account of a kindness the maidservant did for him, and accordingly her release is for his own sake. And some disagree and hold that the permission to free is only for a great need, such as "the mitzva to fulfil the words of the deceased" or in order to complete a minyan, which is a mitzva of the public (Tosafot Gittin 38a, s.v. "kol"; Rashba there 38b).

Even when the injury occurred by mistake, for example if he smeared ointment on his slave's eye to heal it and by mistake blinded it, the slave goes out to freedom. But if he intended to heal one limb, and by mistake injured another limb – he does not go out to freedom. And if the master did not intend this limb but also did not intend the slave's benefit, for example if he threw a stone at an animal and by mistake hit his slave, some say that he does not go out to freedom (Rambam and SA 267:36), and some say that he goes out to freedom (Tosafot and Rosh; Shakh 46). An additional way in which the slave goes out to freedom – when his master renounces ownership of him (mafkiro), and he must give him a bill of manumission, for by the renunciation he is freed from the monetary servitude, and by the bill of manumission the prohibitions specific to a slave are removed from him (SA 267:64).

sections.body_en:
In ancient times the victors in war would do whatever they wished with the vanquished, for in terms of the law they were considered their property. Many of the members of the vanquished people would be killed through public abuse; others were sold as slaves. Many of the women of the vanquished people would be raped without mercy and sold as maidservants or murdered, and in order to save themselves from a cruel death or a life of hunger they used to adorn themselves so that perhaps they would find favour in the eyes of the victorious soldiers and become their concubines. Only in the last few centuries did the attitude toward captives begin to change, yet as recently as about eighty years ago, in the Second World War, soldiers were permitted to rape women during occupation.

In order to raise Israel above the sin of raping the women of the vanquished people, the Torah commanded the soldiers of Israel to fence themselves off from any thought of forbidden relations, as it is stated (Devarim 23:10): "When you go out as a camp against your enemies, you shall guard yourself from every evil thing." But if despite this a soldier desired one of the captive women, so that he would not sin abundantly with a prohibition, the Torah permitted him, within the framework of the law of eshet yefat to'ar (the beautiful captive woman), to come to her in the storm of battle one time, on condition that he undertake to marry her. Afterward he is forbidden to come to her again until the matter of their marriage is arranged. That is to say, if the captive agreed to enter under the wings of the Shekhina through conversion and to marry him – he would convert her immediately, and they had to wait three months until they married, so that if she was pregnant, they would know whether she conceived while she was a gentile or after her conversion.

If she did not want to convert and marry him, he would leave her thirty days to weep and mourn in his house for her parents and for her religion, which she has to leave, and during that time she had to shave her head and let her nails grow. If after the month of mourning the man continued to desire her, and the woman also agreed to convert – she would convert and marry him. And if the man changed his mind and did not want to take her as a wife, he was forbidden to sell her as a maidservant; rather, he must set her free with the status of ger toshav. As it is stated (Devarim 21:14): "And it shall be, if you have no delight in her, then you shall let her go where she will; but you shall not sell her at all for money, you shall not deal with her as a slave, because you have humbled her." While she has the status of ger toshav, one is obligated to treat her with kindness, and an Israelite man is forbidden to take her as a wife without a full conversion. Likewise, if the woman did not want to convert or did not want to marry him, he could keep her with him for up to twelve months, in case she would nevertheless consent to him. If even after twelve months she did not consent, he must set her free with the status of ger toshav (Rambam, Hilkhot Melakhim 8:2-8; 10:12).17

notes_en.en:
In the Yerushalmi, Makkot 2:6, it is explained that according to Rav, the permission regarding eshet yefat to'ar is to come to her one time in the storm of battle, and afterward it is permitted only after she agrees to convert and marries him. And according to Rabbi Yoḥanan there is no permission at all to come to her in the storm of battle; rather, the permission is to take her to his house, and after thirty days she converts and he may take her as a wife. In the Bavli, Kiddushin 21b, it is explained that Rav and Shmuel agree that it is permitted to come to eshet yefat to'ar one time in the storm of battle; and according to Rav, a kohen too was permitted afterward to marry her, while according to Shmuel a kohen is forbidden to marry her. And since Shmuel too agrees with Rav that the permission is to come to her one time in the storm of battle, so wrote most of the Rishonim, among them: the Rambam (Hilkhot Melakhim 8:2), Rabbeinu Tam (Tosafot Kiddushin 22a, s.v. "she-lo"), the Meiri, the Rivash and others. (According to Rashi, Kiddushin there, the halakha follows Rabbi Yoḥanan.) And it is reasonable that the ideal guidance follows Rabbi Yoḥanan, but after the fact, they ruled that it is permitted for a soldier to come to her one time under the conditions explained above.
I wrote above in accordance with the opinion of the Rambam (Hilkhot Melakhim 8:3-7), the Ḥinukh (532) and the Meiri, that only with her consent can she be converted and married. However, according to Rashi (Kiddushin 22a, s.v. "likuḥin"), the Ramban (Devarim 21:12), the Yere'im, the Ritva and the Nimukei Yosef (Yevamot 47b), he can convert her against her will (Ha-mikneh on Kiddushin 22a wrote that even according to Rashi, if he came to her during the war he may not compel her to convert). However, we have already learned in note 13 that even according to their approach it is not fitting to convert her against her will, for if she does not share his faith, there is a concern that she will cause him to stumble in prohibitions. The marriage too must be with her consent (Arukh Ha-shulḥan He-atid, Melakhim 77:9. And according to Zera Avraham 22, he can betroth her against her will).

sections.body_en:
As we have learned, in order to prevent a person from more severe acts, the Torah permitted eshet yefat to'ar under certain conditions; but since the matter runs counter to the moral principles of the Torah, the Torah hinted that use of this permission is liable to bring about bad results. Therefore, in Parashat Ki Tetzei, immediately after the law of eshet yefat to'ar (Devarim 21:10-14), a mitzva is brought that deals with a situation of conflict in the family and a dispute over the inheritance (ibid. 15-17), and after that a mitzva is brought that deals with the stubborn and rebellious son (ben sorer u-moreh) (ibid. 18-21), to teach us that marrying an eshet yefat to'ar is liable to lead to conflicts in the family and to the birth of a stubborn and rebellious son. And so it happened to King David, who took Ma'akha daughter of Talmai king of Geshur as an eshet yefat to'ar, and from the first union between them in the storm of war Tamar was born, and after Ma'akha underwent conversion she bore David Avshalom, who murdered his brother Amnon, and was a stubborn and rebellious son who rebelled against his father and sought to kill him (Sanhedrin 21a). The Sages related (ibid. 107a) that when David fled from Jerusalem before Avshalom his son, his friend Ḥushai the Arkite asked him why he had married an eshet yefat to'ar who gave birth to Avshalom. David answered: "The Torah permitted it," implying that he understood that there was no flaw in it. But Ḥushai answered that he should have paid attention to the passages adjacent to the permission, from which we learn that the matter is undesirable and even dangerous.

The kabbalists explained that there was a certain justice in David's words, for since the Torah permitted eshet yefat to'ar, this implies that within the complicated reality there is a certain rectification in it. And the root of the matter is that following the sin of Adam, souls of Israel were lost among the nations, and some of them returned to Israel within the framework of the law of eshet yefat to'ar. However, since these marriages came about in a very complicated way, they involve suffering, but in the end the holy sparks return to their source. And even over Avshalom, who was the worst son born to an eshet yefat to'ar, David wept and mourned, for he had a good root, and the Sages said that God answered him and raised him from the seven levels of Gehinnom to the World to Come (Sota 10b).18

After all this, since the permission of eshet yefat to'ar is a strained permission for a situation in which the evil inclination dominates a person to the point that if it is not permitted to him in this way – he will act in a far more severe and harsh manner, when it is possible – it is obligatory to prevent it. Therefore today, when thanks to the influence of the morality of the Torah it is agreed throughout the world that an occupied population must not be harmed, and through the means of communication and transportation that have developed it is possible to enforce the laws on soldiers, there is no permission whatsoever to have a marital union without consent and without ḥuppa and kiddushin, and every soldier who transgresses and harms a woman during war must be punished.

notes_en.en: The words of the kabbalists: the Arizal in Likkutei Torah, Ki Tetzei, and Ta'amei Ha-mitzvot there. And so wrote the Or Ha-ḥayim, Devarim 21:11: "The foundation of the matter and its secret is… that through the sin of Adam several precious souls were taken captive in the hand of the Sitra Aḥra (the Other Side), and they are the souls of the converts. And go and learn how many of the great ones of the world come from the nations… He prefaced, 'When you go out to war,' etc., that his going out is for the sake of a mitzva… if he sees an eshet yefat to'ar… that she is the holy soul called 'yefat to'ar' (beautiful of form)… this will awaken you to know that you desired something good." And so wrote Yisrael Kedoshim 6:22-27, and he added that King David prayed for Avshalom and raised him to the Garden of Eden, for indeed his root was in the good. And likewise in Shem Mi-Shmuel, Ki Tetzei 5675: "For all the exiles were for a great need, a descent for the sake of an ascent, like the mitzva of yefat to'ar; therefore God caused it to happen that he would overlook expounding the juxtaposition and would marry a yefat to'ar… in order to bring into actuality the matter of yefat to'ar in general by means of the exile." And see Masoret Ha-giyur 6:14.

sections.body_en:
Members of all the nations can convert, and they are like Israel in every respect. However, regarding four nations the Torah set a restriction on marriage with Israelites, and they are: Ammonites, Moabites, Egyptians and Edomites.

Converts from Ammon and Moav were forbidden in marriage with Israel forever, as it is stated (Devarim 23:4-6): "An Ammonite or a Moabite shall not enter into the congregation of the Lord; even to the tenth generation none of them shall enter into the congregation of the Lord forever. Because they did not meet you with bread and with water on the way, when you came out of Egypt, and because they hired against you Bilam son of Be'or from Petor of Aram Naharayim to curse you. Nevertheless, the Lord your God would not listen to Bilam, but the Lord your God turned the curse into a blessing for you, because the Lord your God loved you."

The children of Ammon and Moav are relatives of Israel, for they are descendants of Lot, the nephew of Avraham our father. Therefore it would have been expected of them that they assist the children of Israel when they went out of Egypt, but even when Israel was hungry and thirsty, they did not meet them with bread and water. The Moabites even hired Bilam to curse Israel (Ramban and Sforno, Devarim 23:5). Since their sin stemmed from bad character traits, the Torah decreed that although they are accepted for conversion, they are forbidden to marry daughters of Israel (Abarbanel there 23:2).

The Sages said that it is a halakha given to Moshe at Sinai (halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai) that the prohibition to marry Moabites and Ammonites applies only to the males and not to the females. And so too one can understand from the reason given in the Torah, that the decree applies to them because they did not meet Israel with bread and water when they came out of Egypt, and it is the males whose way it is to go out to meet travellers. This question arose regarding King David, who was a descendant of Rut the Moabite, and Do'eg the Edomite, who hated David, wanted to accuse him of a flaw in his lineage, for Boaz had been forbidden to marry Rut the Moabite. But Amasa son of Yeter stood against him, and testified to a tradition from Shmuel of Rama that it is a halakha given to Moshe at Sinai that only the males are forbidden and not the females.

Therefore, male converts from Ammon and Moav, as well as their sons and their sons' sons until the end of all generations, can marry only female converts and not daughters of Israel. But female converts from Ammon and Moav, or daughters of converts from Ammon and Moav, can marry even sons of Israel (Yevamot 76b; 77a; Rambam, Hilkhot Issurei Bi'ah 12:18).

Over the many generations that passed, the children of Ammon and Moav intermingled with other nations and the prohibition lapsed. This halakha was ruled on the day that Rabban Gamliel was removed from his position as Nasi, and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya was appointed in his place. As is related in the Mishna (Yadayim 4:4), on that day an Ammonite convert named Yehuda came to the study hall, and asked the Sages whether he was permitted to enter the congregation, that is, to marry a daughter of Israel. Rabban Gamliel answered that it is forbidden, for it is stated (Devarim 23:4): "An Ammonite or a Moabite shall not enter into the congregation of the Lord; even to the tenth generation none of them shall enter into the congregation of the Lord forever." Rabbi Yehoshua answered that it is permitted, for Sennacherib king of Assyria confused and mixed up all the nations (see above, section 9). And therefore many of those who live in the lands of Ammon and Moav and are called Ammonites and Moabites are in fact not children of Ammon and Moav, and no prohibition applies to them. And Rabban Gamliel and the Sages accepted the words of Rabbi Yehoshua, and so it was ruled as halakha (Tosefta Yadayim 2:18; Rambam, Hilkhot Issurei Bi'ah 12:25; SA EH 4:10).

Regarding converts from Edom and Egypt, males and females alike, there is a different restriction: the first and second generations are forbidden to marry Israelites. That is to say, a male or female convert from these nations is permitted to marry converts or descendants of converts, but not sons or daughters of Israel. And so too their sons and daughters, since they are the second generation. But the grandchildren of Edomite or Egyptian converts may marry Israelites. The reason for the prohibition of marriage with members of the first and second generations of the conversion is the wicked behaviour of the peoples of Edom and Egypt toward Israel.

The Egyptians – because of the terrible bondage with which they enslaved Israel with rigour, which the Torah relates at length.

The Edomites are the descendants of Esav, the brother of Yaakov our father, and it would have been fitting for them to behave with brotherhood toward Israel. Therefore, after Israel left Egypt and asked to pass through the land of Edom on their way to the Land of Israel, Moshe our teacher sent messengers to the king of Edom with the request: "Thus says your brother Israel: You know all the travail that has befallen us; how our fathers went down to Egypt, and we dwelt in Egypt a long time, and the Egyptians dealt ill with us and with our fathers. And when we cried to the Lord, He heard our voice, and sent an angel, and brought us out of Egypt; and behold, we are in Kadesh, a city at the edge of your border. Let us pass, I pray you, through your land; we will not pass through field or vineyard, nor will we drink the water of the wells; we will go along the king's highway; we will not turn aside to the right or to the left until we have passed your border." But the king of Edom answered: "You shall not pass through me, lest I come out with the sword against you." And after Israel tried to persuade him to agree, he mobilised his army against them, as it is stated: "And Edom came out against him with a heavy force and with a strong hand. Thus Edom refused to give Israel passage through his border; so Israel turned away from him" (Bamidbar 20:14-21). As a result Israel had to go around the entire land of Edom and lengthen their way to the Land of Israel.

And nevertheless, the Torah commanded not to distance the Edomites and the Egyptians too much, and permitted Israel to convert them and to marry the grandchildren of those of them who convert. The Edomites – because they are the children of Esav, the brother of Yaakov our father. And the Egyptians – because, after all, before the bondage we had good years in Egypt, and even during the bondage, we did not die of hunger and we even were fruitful and multiplied. As it is stated (Devarim 23:8-9): "You shall not abhor an Edomite, for he is your brother; you shall not abhor an Egyptian, because you were a stranger in his land. The children of the third generation that are born to them may enter into the congregation of the Lord."

Since Sennacherib mixed up the nations, those called Edomites do not have the law of an "Edomite," but regarding the Egyptians there is a dispute. Rabbi Yehuda, the disciple of Rabbi Akiva, related that he had a companion among the disciples of Rabbi Akiva, named Minyamin, who was an Egyptian convert. Minyamin said to him: "I am a first-generation Egyptian and I married a first-generation Egyptian woman; I will marry my son to a second-generation Egyptian woman, so that my son's son will be fit to enter the congregation" (Yevamot 76b), implying that the prohibition of an Egyptian entering the congregation was in force in his days. On the other hand, in the Tosefta (Kiddushin 5:4) it is explained that Rabbi Akiva himself told Minyamin his disciple that he erred in this, for the Egyptians too had intermingled with the nations, and therefore he is permitted to marry an Israelite woman like any convert. Apparently, since Egypt was a very great nation, even when the nations intermingled with one another, many members of the Egyptian nation still remained in Egypt, and from this the doubt arose whether the intermingling that took place sufficed to annul the law of an Egyptian from them.19

notes_en.en:
According to the Rambam (Hilkhot Issurei Bi'ah 12:25), like all the nations, the Egyptians too intermingled, and those called "Egyptians" today are not subject to the restriction of an Egyptian convert. And this is also the opinion of the Meiri (Berakhot 28a) and the Baḥ. And according to the Behag, the Rosh (Berakhot 8:4), the Rashba (Yevamot 76b) and the Yam Shel Shlomo (Yevamot 8:24), the Egyptian nation did not intermingle, and the restriction of an Egyptian convert remains upon it. And there is room for doubt whether those who are stringent would be stringent regarding the law of the Egyptians in our days as well. For perhaps, following the Arab conquest and the arrival of members of other nations in Egypt, they too would agree that today they no longer have the law of Egyptians. And perhaps regarding the Copts, who are more closely related to the ancient Egyptians, they would continue to be stringent.
When members of different nations married one another, their children are attributed to the father. Therefore, an Ammonite who married an Egyptian woman – the children are considered Ammonites. And an Egyptian who married an Ammonite woman – the children are Egyptians. But if they converted, one follows the more flawed of the two. Therefore, an Ammonite convert who married an Egyptian female convert – the law of their son is like that of an Ammonite, who is forbidden to marry an Israelite woman forever, whereas the law of their daughter is like that of an Egyptian woman, who is permitted to marry an Israelite only in the third generation. An Egyptian convert who married an Ammonite female convert – the child is Egyptian and forbidden until the third generation (SA EH 4:7-8).

sections.body_en:
A Canaanite who wished to convert could convert and join Israel. However, as a rule the Canaanites were enemies of Israel, both on account of the rivalry over the Land and on account of their being zealous idol worshippers and dissolute in sexual immorality. And therefore Israel was commanded to cut them off, as it is stated (Devarim 7:1-4): "When the Lord your God brings you into the land which you are going to possess, and casts out many nations before you, the Hittite, and the Girgashite, and the Amorite, and the Canaanite, and the Perizzite, and the Ḥivite, and the Jebusite, seven nations greater and mightier than you; and when the Lord your God delivers them before you, and you strike them, you shall utterly destroy them; you shall make no covenant with them, nor show mercy to them. Neither shall you make marriages with them: your daughter you shall not give to his son, nor shall you take his daughter for your son. For he will turn away your son from following Me, that they may serve other gods; so will the anger of the Lord be kindled against you, and He will destroy you quickly."

However, it was a mitzva to call to them for peace and to offer them to join Israel with the status of ger toshav. As the Sages said, already before Israel entered the Land, Yehoshua bin Nun sent the Canaanites three options: 1) to emigrate to another land, 2) to remain in the Land while accepting the seven Noahide commandments and the yoke of the kingdom of Israel within the framework of ger toshav, 3) to fight (Yerushalmi Shevi'it 6:1; above, section 5). And whoever wished could convert and obligate himself in all the mitzvot, and even marry Israelites. For what is stated, "Neither shall you make marriages with them," was said regarding a Canaanite who did not convert. However, regarding the Givonim, who deceived Israel and afterward displayed cruelty, it was decreed that one may not marry them (Rambam, Hilkhot Issurei Bi'ah 12:22-24; above, sections 5-8).20

notes_en.en: However, according to Rabbeinu Tam, it is forbidden to marry Canaanites for all generations, as it is stated: "Neither shall you make marriages with them" (Tosafot Yevamot 79a, s.v. "u-Netinim"). But according to the Rambam (Hilkhot Issurei Bi'ah 12:22), the prohibition is only if they did not convert. And this is also the opinion of Rashi and the Ma'or. And according to the Ramban and Rashba (Ketubot 29a), it was forbidden to marry members of the first generation, but with their children it is permitted. See further above, note 5.

sections.body_en:
Although the Torah commanded to blot out the seed of Amalek, if an Amalekite accepted upon himself to keep the seven Noahide commandments, the law of "Amalek" would cease to apply to him. Not only that, but even when they did not accept upon themselves of their own free will to keep the seven Noahide commandments, before going out to war against them, it is a mitzva to offer them peace. That is, to offer them that they accept upon themselves to keep the seven Noahide commandments, to be subjugated to Israel and to pay them tax, in order to ensure that they do not go back to their old ways of fighting against Israel. If they accepted the terms of peace – one does not fight against them; and if they did not accept – one fights against them until they are destroyed. And even if afterward they wish to change their minds and ask for peace – they are not accepted, for since the war has already begun – one fights them until they are destroyed (Rambam, Hilkhot Melakhim 6:1-4; Kesef Mishneh there).

If an Amalekite wishes to convert, the poskim disagree whether he is accepted. In the opinion of the Rambam (Hilkhot Issurei Bi'ah 12:17) it is permitted to accept him. And so the Sages said, that some of the descendants of Haman the wicked, who was of the seed of Amalek, taught Torah in Bnei Brak (Gittin 57b; Sanhedrin 96b); thus they accepted converts from the seed of Amalek.

And some say that a convert from Amalek is not accepted. And what the Sages said, that some of the descendants of Haman the wicked taught Torah in Bnei Brak, happened by mistake: the court did not know that the one who came before it was of the seed of Amalek, and so they accepted him, and after the fact his conversion is valid. Or an Amalekite went over and joined another nation, and after his Amalekite origin was forgotten he came to convert, and in such a case it is permitted to accept him. Or there was a case in which an Amalekite of the descendants of Haman the wicked raped a Jewish woman, and her son who was born to her from him is considered a Jew, and from him came those teachers of Torah in Bnei Brak. (See Peninei Halakha, Zemanim 14:11, note 12, for a detailed account of the opinions and explanations.)
